LOCAL BUSINESS LICENSE / BUSINESS TAX CERTIFICATE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Retail, LLC · limited liability company

LOCAL BUSINESS LICENSE / BUSINESS TAX CERTIFICATE INFORMATION SHEET — PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This information sheet relates to Acme Retail, LLC, a limited liability company, with a place of business at 100 Market Street, San Diego, CA in the City of San Diego, County of San Diego County, California, engaged in retail clothing and accessories. It describes California's constitutional and statutory framework authorizing California cities and counties to require a local business license or business tax certificate as a condition of operating a business within their jurisdiction — a framework that grants and bounds a city's or county's own licensing power, but that leaves the actual license or certificate, its name, its fee, its renewal cycle, and its application procedure to be enacted, defined, and administered independently by each city and county, rather than by a single state agency or a single statewide statute. This document is not this project's Seller's Permit (California Department of Tax and Fee Administration Registration) Information Sheet, Fictitious Business Name (DBA) Statement, or Foreign LLC/Corporation Qualification document. Those documents concern, respectively: registration with the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration (CDTFA) as a seller of tangible personal property under the state Sales and Use Tax Law; a county-level filing required when a business uses a name other than its true legal name; and an out-of-state entity's registration with the California Secretary of State to transact business in California. A local business license or business tax certificate is a further and separate requirement that a city or county may impose under its own ordinance. A business can complete every one of those other filings and still separately be required, under the ordinance of the specific city or county in which it operates, to hold a local business license or business tax certificate, and a business can be required to hold a local business license or business tax certificate regardless of whether it has made any of those other filings at all. Unlike the seller's permit, California does not have one statewide statute that itself creates a business license requirement, names it, sets its fee, or defines its application procedure; state law instead grants cities and counties broad authority to adopt their own licensing and business-tax ordinances under that authority, and the specific license or certificate name, the businesses and activities it reaches, its fee or tax amount, its renewal cycle, and its application procedure are set locally and vary enormously from one city or county to the next, including among cities and counties within California. This information sheet is informational only. It does not itself obtain a local business license or business tax certificate for Acme Retail, LLC or any other person; it does not determine whether Acme Retail, LLC's specific business or specific location is required to hold one; and it does not state what the City of San Diego, the County of San Diego County, or any other specific city or county actually requires.

CONSTITUTIONAL SOURCE OF LOCAL LICENSING AND REGULATORY AUTHORITY
The ultimate source of a California city's or county's authority to require a local business license or business tax certificate traces to the California Constitution's grant of local "police power." Article XI, Section 7 of the California Constitution states that a county or city may make and enforce, within its own limits, all local, police, sanitary, and other ordinances and regulations that are not in conflict with general laws. This provision does not itself create a business license or business tax requirement, set a fee, or name any specific license; it is the broader constitutional grant of local regulatory and police-power authority on which a city's or county's own business licensing and business-tax ordinances are built, together with the more specific statutory grants described in the other authority clauses of this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A county or city may make and enforce within its limits all local, police, sanitary, and other ordinances and regulations not in conflict with general laws."
  — Cal. Const. art. XI, § 7, California Constitution, Article XI (Local Government), local police power (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%207.&article=XI)
  Known gap: This is one state's constitution, used as real evidence of the ultimate source of a California city's or county's local police power — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific person's or business's obligations, and not a claim that other states' constitutions grant local governments an identical or even similar police power. This clause quotes a single constitutional section, Cal. Const. art. XI, § 7, so no same-section multiple-subsection issue arises here. Article XI, Section 7 is a general grant of local police power, not itself a business license or business tax statute; the actual license or certificate requirements, fees, and procedures that a specific city or county adopts under this and the related statutory grants described elsewhere in this document are set locally and vary by city and county, and this document does not and cannot state what any specific city or county requires. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself obtain a local business license or business tax certificate for the business named in this document or any other person, and it does not determine whether any specific business or jurisdiction requires one.

STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR A CITY TO LICENSE BUSINESS FOR REVENUE AND REGULATION
Two separate California statutes, in two different codes, expressly authorize a city's legislative body to license business activity within its jurisdiction and to set the license fee or tax. Government Code Section 37101(a), part of the Government Code's general provisions on the government of cities, states that a city's legislative body may license, for revenue and regulation, and fix the license tax upon, every kind of lawful business transacted in the city, including shows, exhibitions, and games, and may provide for collecting that license tax by suit or otherwise. Separately, Business and Professions Code Section 16000(a), part of a different code's general business regulations, states that the legislative body of an incorporated city may, in the exercise of its police power and for the purpose of regulation, license any kind of business not prohibited by law that is transacted and carried on within the limits of its jurisdiction, including shows, exhibitions, and lawful games, and may fix the rates of the license fee and provide for its collection by suit or otherwise. These are two independent, overlapping statutory grants of essentially the same core authority — one framed around a city's revenue and regulation power, the other around a city's police power — rather than a single unified statute, and this document does not treat them as the same enactment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The legislative body may license, for revenue and regulation, and fix the license tax upon, every kind of lawful business transacted in the city, including shows, exhibitions, and games."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 37101(a), Government Code, Title 4 (Government of Cities), Chapter 3 (General Powers), business license for revenue and regulation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=37101.)
  "The legislative body of an incorporated city may, in the exercise of its police power, and for the purpose of regulation, as herein provided, and not otherwise, license any kind of business not prohibited by law transacted and carried on within the limits of its jurisdiction, including all shows, exhibitions and lawful games, and may fix the rates of the license fee and provide for its collection by suit or otherwise."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16000(a), Business and Professions Code, Division 7 (General Business Regulations), Chapter 1 (Licensing by Cities), police-power license for regulation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16000.)
  Known gap: These are two of this state's statutes, used as real evidence of California cities' own statutory authority to license business — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific business's obligations, and not a claim that other states grant their cities an identical or even similar licensing power. This clause cites two different statutory sections in two different codes, Cal. Gov. Code § 37101(a) and Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16000(a), each independently verified; they are treated as two separate, overlapping sources of city licensing authority, not as subsections of one section or as one source restated. Neither statute itself names a specific city's license or certificate, sets its fee, or defines its application procedure; the specific license or tax that any given city actually imposes under this authority is set by that city's own ordinance and varies by city, and this document does not and cannot state what any specific city requires. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself obtain a local business license or business tax certificate for the business named in this document or any other person, and it does not determine whether any specific business or city requires one.

STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR A COUNTY TO LICENSE BUSINESS FOR REVENUE AND REGULATION
A California county's authority to license business is set out in a separate statute from the city authority described elsewhere in this document. Revenue and Taxation Code Section 7284(a) states that the board of supervisors of any county may license, for revenue and regulation, and fix the license tax upon, every kind of lawful business transacted in the unincorporated area of the county, including shows, exhibitions, and games, and that the board may provide for collecting that license tax by suit or otherwise. By its own terms, this statute reaches business activity in a county's unincorporated area; it does not itself extend a county's licensing power to activity within an incorporated city located inside that county, which is instead addressed by the city licensing statutes described elsewhere in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The board of supervisors of any county may license, for revenue and regulation, and fix the license tax upon, every kind of lawful business transacted in the unincorporated area of the county, including shows, exhibitions, and games."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 7284(a), Revenue and Taxation Code, Part 1.7 (Additional Local Taxes), Chapter 1.5 (Local Agency Levy Powers and Limitations), county license for revenue and regulation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=7284.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California counties' own statutory authority to license business in unincorporated areas — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific business's obligations, and not a claim that other states grant their counties an identical or even similar licensing power. This clause quotes a single statutory section, Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 7284(a), so no same-section multiple-subsection issue arises here. This statute does not itself name a specific county's license or certificate, set its fee, or define its application procedure; the specific license or tax that any given county actually imposes under this authority is set by that county's own ordinance and varies by county, and this document does not and cannot state what any specific county requires. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself obtain a local business license or business tax certificate for the business named in this document or any other person, and it does not determine whether any specific business or county requires one.

MULTI-JURISDICTION APPORTIONMENT AND THE NONPROFIT/CLERGY EXEMPTION FROM AN INCOME- OR GROSS-RECEIPTS-MEASURED LICENSE TAX
The same statute that grants a city's licensing authority also limits how that authority may be exercised. Government Code Section 37101(b) states that any legislative body, including the legislative body of a charter city, that levies a license tax on a business operating both within and outside its taxing jurisdiction must levy the tax so that the measure of the tax fairly reflects the proportion of the taxed activity actually carried on within that jurisdiction. Government Code Section 37101(c) separately states that no license tax that is measured by a licensee's income or gross receipts, whether levied by a charter or general law city, may apply to a nonprofit organization exempted from taxes under the specified state and federal nonprofit-exemption provisions, or to a minister, clergyperson, Christian Science practitioner, rabbi, or priest of a religious organization granted a federal income tax exemption under Internal Revenue Code Section 501(c)(3) or a successor provision. Business and Professions Code Section 16000(b), the parallel provision tied to the separate police-power licensing statute described elsewhere in this document, states essentially the same nonprofit and clergy exemption from a license fee measured by income or gross receipts.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any legislative body, including the legislative body of a charter city, that levies a license tax pursuant to subdivision (a) upon a business operating both within and outside the legislative body’s taxing jurisdiction, shall levy the tax so that the measure of tax fairly reflects that proportion of the taxed activity actually carried on within the taxing jurisdiction."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 37101(b), Government Code, Title 4 (Government of Cities), Chapter 3 (General Powers), apportionment for multi-jurisdiction business (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=37101.)
  "No license tax levied pursuant to subdivision (a) that is measured by the licensee’s income or gross receipts, whether levied by a charter or general law city, shall apply to any nonprofit organization that is exempted from taxes by Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 23701) of Part 11 of Division 2 of the Revenue and Taxation Code or Subchapter F (commencing with Section 501) of Chapter 1 of Subtitle A of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, or the successor of either, or to any minister, clergyperson, Christian Science practitioner, rabbi, or priest of any religious organization that has been granted an exemption from federal income tax by the United States Commissioner of Internal Revenue as an organization described in Section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code or a successor to that section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 37101(c), Government Code, Title 4 (Government of Cities), Chapter 3 (General Powers), nonprofit and clergy exemption from an income/gross-receipts-measured license tax (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=37101.)
  "No license fee levied pursuant to subdivision (a) that is measured by the licensee’s income or gross receipts, whether levied by a charter or general law city, shall apply to any nonprofit organization that is exempted from taxes by Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 23701) of Part 11 of Division 2 of the Revenue and Taxation Code or Subchapter F (commencing with Section 501) of Chapter 1 of Subtitle A of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, or the successor of either, or to any minister, clergyman, Christian Science practitioner, rabbi, or priest of any religious organization that has been granted an exemption from federal income tax by the United States Commissioner of Internal Revenue as an organization described in Section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code or a successor to that section."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16000(b), Business and Professions Code, Division 7 (General Business Regulations), Chapter 1 (Licensing by Cities), parallel nonprofit and clergy exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16000.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutory framework, used as real evidence of California's own apportionment rule and its nonprofit/clergy exemption from an income- or gross-receipts-measured local license tax or fee — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific business's or organization's obligations, and not a claim that other states impose the same apportionment rule or grant the same exemption. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Gov. Code § 37101(b) and § 37101(c); these two subsections are treated as one source on two related points within a single enactment, not as independent corroborating sources. The clause additionally cites a separate section of a different code, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16000(b), as an independently verified, parallel provision on the nonprofit/clergy exemption tied to that other statute's own police-power licensing authority. Neither statute exempts a nonprofit organization or clergy member from every local business license or business tax certificate requirement — the exemption described here reaches only a license tax or fee measured by income or gross receipts — and any exemption an organization or individual actually receives, and any apportionment a specific city applies, depends on that city's own ordinance, which this document does not and cannot state. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether the business or organization named in this document, or any other specific person or entity, qualifies for this exemption or any local apportionment rule.

CONTRACTOR LICENSE VERIFICATION BEFORE ISSUANCE, AND THE DISABLED-VETERAN PEDDLER EXEMPTION
Two further, unrelated provisions of the same Business and Professions Code chapter that authorizes city business licensing also constrain or exempt from that authority. Business and Professions Code Section 16000(c) states that before a city, including a charter city, issues a business license to a person to conduct business as a contractor, as defined in Business and Professions Code Section 7026, the city must verify that the person is licensed by the Contractors' State License Board. Business and Professions Code Section 16001 separately states that every honorably discharged or honorably relieved soldier, sailor, or marine who served in an enumerated list of wars, who is physically unable to obtain a livelihood by manual labor, and who is a voter of California, may distribute circulars and hawk, peddle, and vend goods, wares, or merchandise the person owns — other than intoxicating liquor — without paying any license tax or fee, whether municipal, county, or state, and that the legislative body must issue that person a license for it without cost.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Before a city, including a charter city, issues a business license to a person to conduct business as a contractor, as defined in Section 7026, the city shall verify that the person is licensed by the Contractors’ State License Board."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16000(c), Business and Professions Code, Division 7 (General Business Regulations), Chapter 1 (Licensing by Cities), contractor license verification before issuance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16000.)
  "Every honorably discharged or honorably relieved soldier, sailor, or marine of the United States or Confederate States who served in the Civil War, any Indian war, the Spanish-American War, any Philippine insurrection, the Chinese Relief Expedition, the World War of 1914 and years following, or World War II, who is physically unable to obtain a livelihood by manual labor, and who is a voter of this state, may distribute circulars, and hawk, peddle, and vend any goods, wares or merchandise owned by him, except spirituous, malt, vinous, or other intoxicating liquor, without payment of any license tax or fee whatsoever, whether municipal, county or state, and the legislative body shall issue to such soldier, sailor or marine, without cost, a license therefor."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16001, Business and Professions Code, Division 7 (General Business Regulations), Chapter 1 (Licensing by Cities), disabled-veteran peddler exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16001.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutory framework, used as real evidence of two specific California constraints on local business licensing power — a contractor-license verification step and a disabled-veteran peddler exemption — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific business's or individual's obligations, and not a claim that other states impose an identical verification step or grant an identical exemption. This clause cites two different sections of the same code, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16000(c) and § 16001, addressing two distinct and unrelated topics; they are treated as two independent points, not as corroborating each other or as one combined rule. Section 16001's enumerated list of wars (through World War II) reflects the statute's text as currently codified and verified on the checkedDate above; this document does not opine on whether, or how, that list has been or should be judicially or administratively applied to a currently living veteran. Neither provision states what license, if any, a specific city actually requires, or how a specific city implements the contractor-verification step or processes a veteran's exemption claim; those specifics are set by each city's own ordinance and procedure. This information sheet is informational only: it does not verify any contractor's license, does not determine whether any specific person qualifies for the exemption described in Section 16001, and does not itself obtain a local business license or business tax certificate, or an exemption from one, for the business or person named in this document or any other person.

NO STATEWIDE FEE CAP FOUND; VOTER-APPROVAL REQUIREMENT FOR LOCAL TAX INCREASES UNDER ARTICLE XIII C
None of the constitutional or statutory provisions reviewed for this document set a statewide dollar cap, statewide rate ceiling, or statewide uniformity standard on the amount a city or county may charge for a local business license or business tax certificate; on the contrary, Government Code Section 37101(a) and Business and Professions Code Section 16000(a), described elsewhere in this document, each state that a city's legislative body "may fix" the license tax or license fee, and Revenue and Taxation Code Section 7284(a) uses the same "may fix" language for a county's board of supervisors. What state law does impose is a procedural constraint on increasing certain local taxes, not a fee ceiling. Article XIII C, Section 2 of the California Constitution, added by a 1996 voter initiative, states that no local government may impose, extend, or increase any general tax unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a majority vote, and separately states that no local government may impose, extend, or increase any special tax unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote. Where a city's or county's business license charge is structured as a tax within the meaning of this constitutional article, rather than as a regulatory fee, this voter-approval requirement can apply to a new levy or a rate increase; the article does not, however, set a numeric ceiling on what a voter-approved local business license tax or business tax certificate fee may be.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "No local government may impose, extend, or increase any general tax unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a majority vote."
  — Cal. Const. art. XIII C, § 2(b), California Constitution, Article XIII C (Voter Approval for Local Tax Levies), voter approval for a general tax (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C)
  "No local government may impose, extend, or increase any special tax unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote."
  — Cal. Const. art. XIII C, § 2(d), California Constitution, Article XIII C (Voter Approval for Local Tax Levies), voter approval for a special tax (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C)
  Known gap: This is one state's constitution and statutes, used as real evidence that California imposes no statewide dollar cap or uniformity standard on a local business license fee or tax, and that a distinct constitutional voter-approval procedure instead applies to certain local tax increases — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific city's or county's charge, and not a claim that other states cap local business license fees or require voter approval to raise them. This clause cites two subsections of the same constitutional section, Cal. Const. art. XIII C, § 2(b) and § 2(d); these two subsections are treated as one source on two related points (general-tax and special-tax voter approval) within a single enactment, not as independent corroborating sources. This clause also references, without re-quoting, the "may fix" language of Cal. Gov. Code § 37101(a), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16000(a), and Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 7284(a), each of which is separately cited and quoted in full in its own clause elsewhere in this document; those references are not offered here as additional independent citations for this clause. Whether a specific city's or county's business license charge is a "general tax," a "special tax," or a regulatory fee outside Article XIII C's voter-approval requirement, and what fee or tax amount a specific city or county actually charges, are determined by that city's or county's own ordinance and enactment history, which this document does not and cannot state. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific local business license charge is subject to Article XIII C's voter-approval requirement, has received the voter approval that requirement demands, or is instead a fee outside that requirement.

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — LOCAL BUSINESS LICENSE / BUSINESS TAX CERTIFICATE INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet regarding Acme Retail, LLC's potential local business license or business tax certificate obligations in the City of San Diego, County of San Diego County, California, was prepared by Jordan T. Reyes.

Executed on April 1, 2026 at San Diego, California.

Signature of Jordan T. Reyes: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes California's constitutional and statutory framework authorizing cities and counties to license or tax businesses operating within their jurisdictions, the multi-jurisdiction apportionment rule and the nonprofit/clergy exemption that limit an income- or gross-receipts-measured license tax, the contractor-license verification step and the disabled-veteran peddler exemption, and the constitutional voter-approval requirement that can apply to a local tax increase. It is not a business license application, business tax certificate, or any other form issued by any city or county; it does not itself obtain a local business license or business tax certificate for Acme Retail, LLC or any other person; it does not constitute legal advice; and it does not determine whether Acme Retail, LLC's specific business, or the specific City of San Diego or County of San Diego County in which it operates, requires one, or what fee, form, or procedure would apply. The current business license or business tax certificate name, fee, form, and procedure applicable to Acme Retail, LLC's specific location are set and published by the applicable city and/or county, not by this document.]

expectedJSON.body: None of the constitutional or statutory provisions reviewed for this document set a statewide dollar cap, statewide rate ceiling, or statewide uniformity standard on the amount a city or county may charge for a local business license or business tax certificate; on the contrary, Government Code Section 37101(a) and Business and Professions Code Section 16000(a), described elsewhere in this document, each state that a city's legislative body "may fix" the license tax or license fee, and Revenue and Taxation Code Section 7284(a) uses the same "may fix" language for a county's board of supervisors. What state law does impose is a procedural constraint on increasing certain local taxes, not a fee ceiling. Article XIII C, Section 2 of the California Constitution, added by a 1996 voter initiative, states that no local government may impose, extend, or increase any general tax unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a majority vote, and separately states that no local government may impose, extend, or increase any special tax unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote. Where a city's or county's business license charge is structured as a tax within the meaning of this constitutional article, rather than as a regulatory fee, this voter-approval requirement can apply to a new levy or a rate increase; the article does not, however, set a numeric ceiling on what a voter-approved local business license tax or business tax certificate fee may be.
